#Task: load tidyverse, tidytext, rio, janitor libraries

#Task: Tokenize the hlead column

Copy the code from the in-class bigrams exercise and tokenize just the hlead column from your dataframe

Hint: you're changing just one variable

#Answer: Changed the name of the data file to Xinjiang_women and renamed stories_tokenized to Hlead_tokenized as well as replaced "stories" with "Hlead" in the unnest_tokens field. I tried two versions but received the same results, which I explained below in memo.

#Version1

```{r}
Xinjiang_Women %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, Hlead)
```
#Version2

```{r}
Hlead_tokenized <- Xinjiang_Women %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, Hlead)

Hlead_tokenized
```


#Task: Remove stopwords and count the words
#Answer: Renamed the code to Hlead_tokenized, removed stopwords 

```{r}

data(stop_words)

Hlead_tokenized <- Hlead_tokenized %>%
  anti_join(stop_words, by = c("word" = "word")) %>%
  filter(word != "temp_file") %>%
  filter(word != "stories_corpus") %>%
  filter(!grepl('[0-9]', word))

```

#Asnwer: counting the words

```{r}
Hlead_word_ct <- Hlead_tokenized %>%
  count(word, sort=TRUE)

head(story_word_ct, 20)
```

#Task: Create Bigrams
#Answer: Renamed datafile to mine, replaced "stories" with "Hlead". 

```{r}
bigrams <- Xinjiang_Women %>%
  unnest_tokens(bigram, Hlead, token="ngrams", n=2)

bigrams


```

#Task: Filter out stop words.
#Answer: done, renamed decade to "post2015", top 10 bigrams are below.

```{r}
data(stop_words)

bigrams1 <- bigrams %>%
  filter(!is.na(bigram)) |> 
  separate(bigram, c("word1", "word2"), sep = " ")

bigrams2 <- bigrams1 %>%
  filter(!word1 %in% stop_words$word) %>%
  filter(!word2 %in% stop_words$word) |> 
  count(word1, word2, sort = TRUE) |> 
  mutate(decade = "post2015") # label the range of your data

head(bigrams2, 100)
```

#Task: Write 250 words about what your learned analyzing the list of tokens and bigrams. Include questions about the process and any difficulties you encountered.

#Memo: 224 words

This exercise is useful to see a quick overview of the most frequent words in the data that you have. It was good to work on my own dataset!

One interesting result from this data analysis is that #top4 bigram is "birth, control," which is a common coverage linked to women from this region who are forcibly sterilized or made to have abortions. When it comes to single words, most of them are predictable, but #7 is "genocide", which can also tell about the coverage of those women in the media.

Overall, I can see value in analyzing bigrams because they show the most frequent word pairings in the data file, and they can tell you something when you want to understand the specifics of the news content. I am not so sure about single words; in this context, they didn't show as much value as bigrams. However, with a different (bigger) dataset, they may prove to be a valuable source of information. 

What I did not quite understand is the first part of tokenizing. When I run my code, it just shows me full Hleads, full sentences. It is not until I count the (single) words that I see the separation. I have re-read the tidy text mining chapter to understand, but maybe I missed something in my code; I am not sure.
